text: Every integration so far has assumed standard HTTPS, where only the external server proves its identity to ServiceNow. This lesson covers two options for when that one-directional trust isn't enough, or isn't even available: mutual TLS and API keys.

In standard HTTPS, the server presents a certificate and the client verifies it — the client's own identity is proven separately, through whatever Authentication Profile is configured. Mutual TLS changes that: both sides present and verify certificates. ServiceNow also presents its own client certificate, and the external server verifies it before accepting the connection at all. If either certificate doesn't check out, the handshake fails before a single request runs.

That's real overhead, so mutual TLS isn't the default choice for a routine integration. It shows up specifically for highly sensitive integrations — financial systems, government systems — where certificate-based identity verification on both ends is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Not every external API supports OAuth or mutual TLS. A lot of real-world APIs authenticate with nothing more than an API key: a shared secret string passed in a custom header, commonly something like X-API-Key, configured right on the REST Message's HTTP Headers rather than through an Authentication Profile.

API keys are less standardized and generally less secure than OAuth. Every vendor picks its own header name and revocation process, and most implementations have no built-in expiration and no scope model — a leaked key is often all-or-nothing access until someone manually rotates it, the same weakness Basic Auth has. The honest reason they're still worth knowing: plenty of partners simply don't offer anything stronger.

Three real options, three different jobs: OAuth as the default whenever it's supported, mutual TLS when certificate verification on both ends is required, and API keys when the partner offers nothing else. Next up: the Authentication Lab, walking a real integration decision through all three.
